Maladaptive Strategies.value: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
Being alone in a room or building
Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The people responsible have faced no consequences
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, nocturnal checking for one's own immediate physical safety is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it introduces a more direct personal-danger threat theme that is not otherwise represented in triggers or memory. The triggers and memory items are centered on reminders of the loved one's trauma/loss rather than the patient's own current physical danger, so this specific item is the least coherent threat item.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: Self-blame based on one's character can occur after a loved one's trauma, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals focused on institutional failure and lack of accountability, which externalize blame to others. This is not impossible, but this item is the most internally tensioned within the appraisal node and less clearly linked to the rest of the profile than guilt on recall would be.

vignette: Kamran's eyes still scan the crowded room, his mind on high alert, even after all these years. As an actor, he's accustomed to being in the spotlight, but now the mere thought of stepping into a packed auditorium makes his skin crawl. It's been five years since his wife, Sarah, was killed in a tragic accident involving a faulty elevator at their son's school. The incident left Kamran with scars that run far deeper than the physical ones. That day is etched in his memory like a series of disjointed photographs. He recalls the sound of children crying, the screech of metal twisting, and the eerie silence that followed. The images flash through his mind in fragmented pieces – he remembers rushing to the scene, seeing the mangled elevator car, and being told that Sarah was gone. But there's a haze around the edges, as if his brain is shielding him from the full horror. The aftermath of the tragedy was a blur of condolences, funeral arrangements, and numbness. Kamran went through the motions, playing the role of the grieving husband, but beneath the surface, he was consumed by self-blame and guilt. He couldn't shake the feeling that he should have done more to prevent the accident, that he'd been too trusting of the school's safety record. The weight of his inaction crushed him. As time passed, Kamran began to notice changes within himself. He found it increasingly difficult to concentrate on his work, often getting stuck on a single line or struggling to recall entire scenes. Simple tasks became Herculean challenges. His friends and family tried to reassure him that he was safe, but Kamran couldn't shake the feeling of unease that had taken up residence in his mind. He started avoiding crowds, finding excuses to skip social gatherings and performances. The sound of children laughing or playing would send a shiver down his spine, transporting him back to that terrible day. Even the media – once a trusted source of information – became a minefield. Kamran would catch snippets of news stories about similar accidents or near-misses, and his mind would spiral into catastrophic scenarios. In an attempt to cope with these emotions, Kamran developed a people-pleasing habit. He'd agree to take on roles he wasn't suited for, attend events that made him anxious, all in the hopes of avoiding being alone with his thoughts. Being by himself, even in a quiet room, felt like an invitation for his darkest fears to resurface. As the months went by, Kamran's relationships began to fray. His friends and family grew tired of his constant cancellations and mood swings. His agent started to lose patience with his lack of focus on set. The weight of his guilt and shame threatened to consume him whole. Kamran knows he needs help, but it's hard for him to trust anyone – including himself. He fears that therapy will only serve as a reminder of his failures, that he'll be forced to confront the what-ifs and maybes that haunt him still. But with each passing day, the pain becomes more unbearable, and Kamran is starting to realize that he can't keep running from his demons forever. He's taken the first step by seeking help, but as he sits in the therapist's office, waiting for their session to begin, Kamran can't shake the feeling that he'll never be able to forgive himself – or others – for what happened.
